## AudioVisualizer.kt { #audiovisualizer-kt }

The recorded-audio waveform player: a zoomable, seekable view of a recording, as one
self-contained HTML fragment for a box output.

It shows audio that already exists, rather than a spectrum or a live meter, with the interaction
an editor expects (wheel to zoom, drag to pan, click to seek, a playhead that tracks playback)
and the browser's own transport underneath.

What it draws is a min/max envelope of the *visible* window, not the whole file decimated. Where
a server can summarise a window (`AudioVisualizerSource.waveformUrl` — Field Audio's waveform
endpoint, for instance) the component asks for one envelope per view, so an hour-long recording
costs the same as a bar of it; where there is no server it decodes the clip in the browser and
does the same arithmetic locally. Min/max rather than an average is what keeps a single-sample
click visible in a window drawn at 1000 points.

Start from `Box.displayAudio` for a URL, `Box.displayAudioSamples` for a `FloatArray` you
generated, or `Box.displayAudioBytes` for an encoded clip you have in memory.

## interactionnets.kt { #interactionnets-kt }

Interaction nets as a live-codeable medium: a graph whose nodes rewrite each other wherever two of them
touch principal port to principal port, with a DSL for building nets, a rule language for the rewrites, a
scheduler that decides which collision fires next, and a force-directed layout so you can watch it happen.

Start at `net` to build one, `rules` to say how it rewrites, [`Reducer`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-reducer) to run it, and `Net.toFLines` or
`Box.showInteractionNet` to look at it. [`Lambda`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-lambda) is a ready-made vocabulary (APP, LAM, DUP, ERASE, ROOT,
VAR, CONST) with its own rule book, if you want the classical behaviour rather than your own.

A compact, single-file interaction-net playground meant to be easy to lift into a larger codebase,
but also meant to be a fertile computational substrate for live coding art.

What is in here:
- a small in-memory interaction-net graph model
- a Kotlin DSL for building whole nets and reusable graph fragments
- two rewrite styles:
    1) a declarative "automatic rewiring" DSL built around ext(side, aux)
    2) an escape hatch for arbitrary custom rewrites in ordinary Kotlin
- configurable active-pair scheduling
- a simple force-directed layout with incremental seeding of rewrite RHS nodes at the LHS center
- FLine/output rendering plus SVG export for quick inspection
- a small lambda-oriented bundle including APP, LAM, DUP, ERASE, ROOT, VAR, CONST

Design intent:
- Keep the core tiny and hackable.
- Make the common case pleasant without removing low-level control.
- Be explicit about where the model is still incomplete.
- Treat the system less like a theorem prover and more like a graph chemistry / reactive medium.

The artistic framing:
This file is not most interesting as a route to "real lambda calculus". It is more interesting as a
local, spatial, rewiring-based substrate for live coding. In that framing:

- principal ports are not just logical redex triggers; they are collision points, activation sites,
  rhythmic contact surfaces
- auxiliary ports are not just variables; they can be treated as tension channels, color buses,
  growth directions, continuation hooks, memory strands, or signal paths
- rewrite rules are not merely reductions; they are local laws of motion, branching, fusion,
  mutation, decay, reflection, gating, or pulse propagation
- active-pair scheduling is not merely evaluation order; it is rhythm, phrasing, emphasis, groove,
  cascade control
- layout is not merely display; it is motion memory and can become part of the meaning of the system

DUP and ERASE in this context:
DUP and ERASE are useful here less as strict lambda-calculus machinery and more as artistic growth and
decay primitives.

- DUP can mean branching, echo, motif propagation, splitting a line of force into two descendants,
  or generating two related but diverging futures
- ERASE can mean fade, pruning, absorption, dissipation, culling, or a sink that removes pressure from
  a local region

In a more expressive live system, DUP does not need to be perfectly literal duplication. It can create
two descendants with slight positional offsets, inherited state, hue drift, phase drift, timing skew,
energy split, or generation markers. Likewise ERASE does not need to be instantaneous deletion; it can
become gradual attenuation, shrinkage, or multi-frame disappearance.

Why this is promising for live coding art:
- Local causality: every visible change comes from a small neighborhood interaction.
- Spatial meaning: the graph is data and choreography at once.
- Compositionality: a small table of rewrite laws can yield rich large-scale behavior.
- Performability: rules, scheduler, layout constants, render mapping, and node injection can all be
  changed while the system is running.

Activation order as an instrument:
Reduction order is a first-class artistic control. A deterministic scheduler can feel mechanical;
randomized scheduling can shimmer; energy-biased or cursor-biased scheduling can create bursts,
avalanches, attraction, or spotlighting. Treat scheduling as part of the score.

Layout as part of computation:
The incremental layout already gives new RHS nodes a positional memory by seeding them at the centroid
of the consumed active pair before relaxation. That idea can be pushed further. Rewrite rules can read
or influence geometry; branch direction can depend on current edge angle; replication distance can
depend on energy; eligibility can depend on local spatial conditions; layout velocity can feed rendering
or sound. The graph need not be computed first and visualized second.

A "wet" semantics is often better than a perfectly dry one:
For artistic purposes, clean instantaneous replacement is sometimes less interesting than sticky,
physicalized replacement. Newly created nodes can inherit centroid and velocity. Consumed edges can
leave ghosts. Erased nodes can decay over a few frames. Duplicated nodes can repel strongly at birth
and then settle. Rules can emit transient sparks or decorative residues. These choices improve visual
legibility and expressiveness during rapid change.

The next high-leverage extension is per-node state:
Adding a small mutable state record to each node would make the substrate much richer. Examples:

    data class State(
        var energy: Double = 1.0,
        var phase: Double = 0.0,
        var hue: Double = 0.0,
        var age: Double = 0.0
    )

Then rewrite rules can split energy on DUP, accumulate age, drift hue, mutate phase, and directly map
these quantities to radius, stroke weight, opacity, curvature, synthesis parameters, or triggering.

Rendering and sound hooks:
A rewrite can be more than a topology update. In a live system it is natural for a rewrite to also emit
events such as "flash this edge", "trigger a note", "spawn a particle", "increase camera pull", or
"mark this component active". That turns graph rewriting into the event engine for an audiovisual system.

Useful node archetypes for an artistic palette:
- Pulse   : propagates motion or activation
- DUP     : bifurcates structure or motive
- ERASE   : consumes / attenuates / prunes
- Delay   : holds activity for N frames or beats
- Gate    : conditionally passes or blocks interaction
- Mirror  : swaps neighborhoods / reflects flow
- Fuse    : merges strands
- Noise   : injects stochastic variation
- Anchor  : spatial stabilizer
- Bloom   : expands into decorative local structure

A note on rigor:
This file adds DUP and ERASE agents in the usual explicit-resource spirit, but it is not trying to be a
complete optimal reducer. There is no full fan/fan commuting story, no full lambda frontend, and no
claim of theoretical completeness. That is deliberate. The value here is as a hackable medium with:

- topology that changes
- space that remembers
- order that matters
- small laws that create style

In other words: treat this as a graph chemistry for live coding.

### LayoutConfig { #interactionnets-kt-layoutconfig }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">LayoutConfig</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">repulsion</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">2500.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">springLength</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">90.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">springStrength</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.015</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">damping</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.82</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">timeStep</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">jitter</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">8.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">clampStep</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">20.0</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L165)

The knobs on the force-directed layout that `Net.relax` runs — every node pushing every other apart, every edge pulling its two ends together.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">repulsion</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | How hard every node pushes every other away. Falls off as `1/d²`, so it sets the empty space between unconnected nodes without much affecting connected ones. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">springLength</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | The distance an edge is happy at, in position units. The quickest single knob for the overall scale of the picture. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">springStrength</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | How strongly an edge pulls back toward `springLength`. Large values make the net rigid and jittery. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">damping</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Velocity retained per step. Below 1 is what makes the simulation settle at all; toward 1 it wobbles for far longer, and at 1 it never stops. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">timeStep</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Integration step. Scales both the velocity update and the movement, so raising it is a faster but less stable simulation. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">jitter</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Stored but **unused** by the current layout step — new nodes get their initial scatter from `Net.create` instead. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">clampStep</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Per-step speed limit, in position units. What stops two nearly coincident nodes from firing each other off the canvas. |

### NodeState { #interactionnets-kt-nodestate }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">NodeState</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">energy</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">phase</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">hue</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">age</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">scalars</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MutableMap</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">&gt;</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">linkedMapOf</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L203)

The mutable per-node payload that turns a bare interaction net into something worth watching: four named quantities the renderer already reads, plus `scalars` for anything else you want to carry.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">energy</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Drives node radius when drawn, and is what the energy-biased [`PairSelectors`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-pairselectors) rank pairs by. Every operation here floors it at 0, but nothing caps it. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">phase</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Carried and split, but **nothing in this file interprets it** — yours to use, though the renderer does fall back to it for a node's port angle when the node has no connected neighbours. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">hue</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Drives colour, as a fraction of a turn. Wrapped at render time rather than here, so it may drift far outside `0..1` and that is fine. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">age</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Advanced only by `Net.incrementAges`, in whatever unit you pass it — so age runs on the clock you choose. Nudges drawn lightness. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">scalars</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MutableMap</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | Room for your own named quantities. Deep-copied by `copyDeep` and blended key-wise by `blend`, where a key missing from one side counts as 0. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">copyDeep</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">NodeState</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L221) | An independent copy, `scalars` map included, so later mutation of either cannot reach the other. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">evolved</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">energyScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">energyBias</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">phaseShift</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">hueShift</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">ageDelta</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">NodeState</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L236) | A copy with the four quantities moved on — the "one node becomes one node, a little different" step for a rewrite rule to hand its replacement. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">split</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">parts</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">branch</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">attenuation</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">hueSpread</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">phaseSpread</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">ageDelta</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">NodeState</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L259) | One branch's share of this state when a node divides into `parts` — the state side of a DUP-style rewrite. |

### PortKind { #interactionnets-kt-portkind }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">PortKind</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L317)

Which of a node's two kinds of port this is — and therefore whether an edge through it can *react*.

Constants: `PRINCIPAL`, `AUXILIARY`.

### AgentType { #interactionnets-kt-agenttype }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">AgentType</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">auxPorts</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L326)

A kind of node: a name to match rules against, and how many auxiliary ports its instances get.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">arity</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L328) | Total port count: the auxiliaries plus the one principal port. |

### Port { #interactionnets-kt-port }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">Port</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">constructor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">node</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Node</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">index</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">kind</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">PortKind</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L339)

One port on one node — the thing edges connect. Port 0 is always the principal port and `1..auxPorts` the auxiliaries, which is why `Node.aux` takes a 0-based index and adds one for you.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">node</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Node</span></code> | The node this port belongs to. A port never moves between nodes. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">index</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Position in the node's `ports` list: 0 is the principal port, `1..auxPorts` the auxiliaries. Note this is the raw index, one more than the number `Node.aux` takes. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">kind</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">PortKind</span></code> | Whether this is the one reactive port or an inert auxiliary. Fixed when the node is created. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">id</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L349) | `"<nodeId>:<portIndex>"` — the stable string identity [`Net`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-net) uses for its adjacency index. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">override</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">toString</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L352) | The port's `id`. |

### Node { #interactionnets-kt-node }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">Node</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">constructor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">id</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">type</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AgentType</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">state</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">NodeState</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">NodeState</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L362)

One node in a net: an [`AgentType`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-agenttype), a stable `id`, a fixed list of `ports` and a mutable [`NodeState`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-nodestate).

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">id</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | Unique within its net and never reused, so a [`ReductionStep`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-reductionstep)'s removed ids stay unambiguous after the fact. Minted as `type_n` by [`IdSource`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-idsource) unless you named it. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">type</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AgentType</span></code> | Which kind of agent this is — what rules match on, and what fixes the port count. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">state</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">NodeState</span></code> | This node's mutable payload. `Net.create` copies whatever you pass, so two nodes never share one by accident; a rewrite rule must copy it explicitly. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">ports</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Port</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L373) | All of this node's ports, principal first at index 0, then the auxiliaries in order. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">principal</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Port</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L381) | This node's one reactive port. Wire two of these together and you have an [`ActivePair`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-activepair). |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">aux</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">i</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Port</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L388) | Auxiliary port `i`, numbered from **0** — so `aux(0)` is `ports[1]`. |

| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">infix</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">PortRef</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">to</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">other</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">PortRef</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1460) | `principal(a) to aux(b, 0)` — wires two ports **inside** the replacement. | [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">reconnect</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">newPort</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">PortRef</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">oldPeer</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Port</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1471) | Attaches a replacement node's port to one of the loose ends the deleted pair left behind — this is how the surrounding net stays connected. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">reconnect</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">newPort</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">PortRef</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">nodeOrdinal</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">auxIndex</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1480) | The same as the other `reconnect`, naming the loose end by which node of the pair it belonged to (0 = first, 1 = second) and which of its auxiliary ports — the shorter form, and the one that matches `ext(...)` in the automatic DSL. Silently does nothing if that port was free. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">passthrough</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">a</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Port</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Port</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1490) | Wires two of the pair's loose ends **directly to each other**, bypassing the deleted nodes entirely — how you write an ERASE or a plain "these two were connected through me, now connect them" rule. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">emit</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">kind</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">magnitude</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">ctx</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">pairEnergy</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">at</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec2</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">ctx</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">center</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">data</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Map</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">&gt;</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">emptyMap</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1500) | Records a [`RewriteEvent`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-rewriteevent) for whoever is watching the reduction — a flash, a note, a particle. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">build</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">RewriteResult</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1510) | The assembled [`RewriteResult`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-rewriteresult). `RuleBook.rule` calls this for you. |

### RewriteResult { #interactionnets-kt-rewriteresult }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">RewriteResult</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">constructor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">fragment</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">NetFragment</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">NetFragment</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">reconnections</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MutableList</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Pair</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">PortRef</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">Port</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">&gt;</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">mutableListOf</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">passthroughs</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MutableList</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Pair</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Port</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">Port</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">&gt;</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">mutableListOf</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">events</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MutableList</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">RewriteEvent</span><span class="p">&gt;</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">mutableListOf</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1521)

What a rule body produces: the replacement subgraph, how it attaches to the loose ends, which loose ends were joined to each other, and any events emitted.

### RewriteRule { #interactionnets-kt-rewriterule }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">RewriteRule</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">signature</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">PairSignature</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">rewrite</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">PairContext</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">RewriteResult</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1537)

One law of motion: a name, the pair of types it fires on, and a function from the collision to its replacement.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | What this law is called. Appears in every [`ReductionStep`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-reductionstep) it produces, so make it readable. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">signature</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">PairSignature</span></code> | The pair of agent types this fires on, matched in either order. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">rewrite</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">PairContext</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">RewriteResult</span></code> | Called afresh on **every** firing with that collision's context, so the replacement can depend on energy, geometry and velocity rather than being a fixed template. |

### AutoEndpoint { #interactionnets-kt-autoendpoint }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">sealed</span> <span class="k">interface</span> <span class="nc">AutoEndpoint</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1554)

One end of a wire in the automatic-rewiring DSL: either a port of a node the rule is creating ([`InternalEndpoint`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-internalendpoint)) or one of the loose ends the deleted pair left behind ([`ExternalEndpoint`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-externalendpoint)).

### InternalEndpoint { #interactionnets-kt-internalendpoint }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">InternalEndpoint</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">ref</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">PortRef</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AutoEndpoint</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1557)

A port of a node this rule is creating. Produced by `principal(...)` / `aux(...)` in an [`AutoRuleBuilder`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-autorulebuilder).

### ExternalEndpoint { #interactionnets-kt-externalendpoint }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">ExternalEndpoint</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">nodeOrdinal</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">auxIndex</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AutoEndpoint</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1565)

A loose end of the *old* pair: auxiliary port `auxIndex` of pair node `nodeOrdinal` (0 = first, 1 = second).

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">AutoRuleBuilder</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">constructor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">ctx</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">PairContext</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1584)

Ignored if that port was free. |

Same as `RewriteBuilder.emit`. |

### RuleBook { #interactionnets-kt-rulebook }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">RuleBook</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1708)

The table of rewrite laws a net runs under — declare rules into it with `rule` and `autoRule`, and it answers "does anything apply to these two nodes".

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">rule</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">left</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AgentType</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">right</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AgentType</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">rewrite</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">RewriteBuilder</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">PairContext</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Unit</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1718) | Declares a rule with the full-control [`RewriteBuilder`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-rewritebuilder) body — you say what nodes appear and explicitly reconnect or pass through each of the old pair's loose ends. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">autoRule</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">left</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AgentType</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">right</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AgentType</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">rewrite</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AutoRuleBuilder</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">PairContext</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Unit</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1736) | Declares a rule with the declarative [`AutoRuleBuilder`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-autorulebuilder) body — you list the connections and the builder works out which are internal, which reattach the old pair's loose ends and which splice two of them together. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">find</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">a</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Node</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Node</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">RewriteRule</span><span class="o">?</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1749) | The first rule that fires on these two nodes, or null. `findMatch` when you also need the orientation. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">findMatch</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">a</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Node</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Node</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">RuleMatch</span><span class="o">?</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1757) | The first rule matching these two nodes, together with the binding that puts them in the rule's own order. |

### ActivationOrder { #interactionnets-kt-activationorder }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">ActivationOrder</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1779)

The ready-made choices for *which* of several possible reactions fires next — reduction order as a dial.

Constants: `FIRST_FOUND`, `LEFTMOST_BY_ID`, `RIGHTMOST_BY_ID`, `RANDOM`, `HIGHEST_PAIR_ENERGY`, `LOWEST_PAIR_ENERGY`.

### PairCandidate { #interactionnets-kt-paircandidate }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">PairCandidate</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">pair</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ActivePair</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">match</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">RuleMatch</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">context</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">PairContext</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1795)

One reaction that *could* happen this step: the active pair, the rule that matched it, and the fully built [`PairContext`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-paircontext) the rule would be given.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">rule</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">RewriteRule</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1797) | The rule that would fire. Shorthand for `match.rule`. |

### PairSelector { #interactionnets-kt-pairselector }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="k">interface</span> <span class="nc">PairSelector</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1807)

The scheduler: given every reaction that could fire, pick one — or return null to stop the reduction.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">select</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">net</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Net</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">candidates</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">PairCandidate</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">PairCandidate</span><span class="o">?</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1814) | Choose the reaction to fire, or null to stop. |

### PairSelectors { #interactionnets-kt-pairselectors }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">PairSelectors</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1818)

The stock [`PairSelector`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-pairselector)s — the schedulers [`ActivationOrder`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-activationorder) names, plus two that it does not.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">firstFound</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1820) | Takes whichever candidate came first out of the edge set. Cheapest, and the most mechanical-looking. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">leftmostById</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1824) | Prefers the pair containing the alphabetically smallest node id — deterministic, and roughly oldest-first, since ids are minted in creation order. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">rightmostById</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1827) | Prefers the pair containing the alphabetically largest node id — deterministic, and roughly newest-first. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">highestPairEnergy</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/interactionnets/#L1830) | Always fires the hottest pair. Tends to produce avalanches and to keep activity concentrated in one region. |

## keyframeBrowser.kt { #keyframebrowser-kt }

Reading a *collection* of saved keys the way [`KeyframeScope`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-keyframescope) reads one: a glob of key files in,
a slot-major summary out.

### Why slot-major

A directory of keys is a sparse three-axis cube — file × version × slot — and only one of those
axes tells you anything you did not already know. You know your file names. What you cannot see
from a directory listing is which slots you actually kept pushing on, which have been frozen since
the first save, and which are missing from half the files because the scope grew a target after
they were written. So this pivots to slots, and every summary here is computed across files
rather than within one.

### What `load` reads

`load` decodes each matched file straight to [`KeyDTO`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-keydto) rather than going through
`KeyframeScope.loadKey`, which fills `KeyframeScope.missingKey` defaults for names a file lacks —
exactly right when you are about to apply a key and exactly wrong when you are trying to *see*
which names a file lacks. The browser wants the file as written.

Version history is read lazily. `load` calls `KeyframeScope.keyVersions` for each file, which
lists a directory and parses one manifest, but it does not open the numbered snapshots. Those are
only read when `slotHistory` is asked for one slot's trajectory — a hundred saves of ten files is
a thousand files, and no one wants that on open.

### Failure is per-file

A collection with one unparseable file still browses. `load` records the failure in
`KeyframeCollection.problems` and carries on, so one bad file does not make the other nine
invisible.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/keyframeBrowser.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/keyframeBrowser/)

## lambdaterms.kt { #lambdaterms-kt }

λ-terms as a front end to the interaction nets in `interactionnets.kt`: text in, a reduced net out, a term back.

The shortest useful thing is `LambdaTerms.normalise`, which runs parse, compile, reduce and readback in one call:

    val run = LambdaTerms.normalise("(\\m n f x. m f (n f x)) (\\f x. f x) (\\f x. f (f x))")
    run.printed   // "λa. λb. a (a (a b))", Church three, from add one two
    run.steps     // how many reactions it took

Two public names sit behind that. [`Term`](visualization.md#lambdaterms-kt-term) is the syntax tree, with `Var`, `Lam` and `App` nested inside it so that
`Term.Lam("x", Term.Var("x"))` reads as what it is and none of the three short names leaks into `afield.stdlib`.
[`LambdaTerms`](visualization.md#lambdaterms-kt-lambdaterms) is everything done to one: parsing, printing, compilation to the [`Lambda`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-lambda) agent vocabulary, readback,
and the reference evaluator the net's answer is checked against.

Every answer here is computed twice. The net is one route; `LambdaTerms.referenceNormalOrder` is the other, and
reduces by capture-avoiding substitution with no nets and no sharing anywhere in it, so the two routes share no
machinery beyond the term type. `LambdaTerms.corpus` is the set of closed terms both are run over.

The file lands on the Visualization page because a finished run keeps the [`Net`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-net) it reduced, and `Net.toFLines`
draws that net with its active pairs emphasised.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/lambdaterms.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/lambdaterms/)

## Colormaps.kt { #colormaps-kt }

The colour vocabulary the visualization helpers share: [`Color4`](visualization.md#colormaps-kt-color4), a `[0,1]`-component colour value
with no dependencies, and [`Colormaps`](visualization.md#colormaps-kt-colormaps), eight named ramps that can be sampled at any parameter.

A ramp here is a short table of evenly-spaced control points rather than a 256-entry lookup table
(nine colours for each of the matplotlib maps, seventeen for turbo, three for the house
cyan→orange), and `Colormaps.sampleStops` interpolates linearly between them. A caller that
colours one pixel at a time builds its own table from that: `showHeatmap` quantises the ramp into
1024 entries once per image rather than interpolating per pixel.

Names are matched after trimming and lowercasing, `gray`, `greys` and `cyan-orange` are aliases,
and an unknown name raises with `Colormaps.names` in the message rather than falling back to a
default. RectSL's `colormap` and `cmap` words, `showHeatmap` and the imaging visualizers all take
that same vocabulary, so a ramp named in one place is the same ramp in another.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/visualization/Colormaps.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/visualization/Colormaps/)

### Colormaps { #colormaps-kt-colormaps }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">Colormaps</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/visualization/Colormaps/#L67)

Perceptually-uniform colormaps as named colour ramps — matplotlib's viridis / magma / plasma / inferno, Google's turbo, Kenneth Moreland's coolwarm diverging map, and a plain grayscale. Each map is a table of evenly-spaced RGB control points taken from the published data (the viridisLite 9-class swatches for the matplotlib family, the turbo_srgb_floats LUT sampled every 16th entry, Moreland's cool→warm table); `sampleStops` interpolates linearly between them. This is reusable domain code — the single source of truth for the `showHeatmap` visualizer and RectSL's `colormap`/`cmap`, `bars`, `heat`, and `scatter` words, and directly callable from Kotlin.

## DataFrameCharts.kt { #dataframecharts-kt }

A typed frame, charting its own columns.

`DataFrameVisualizer` already teaches a frame to render as a [`Table`](visualization.md#tables-kt-table) for `.h` and to stream its
rows for `.h2`, which is the right compact form: a frame is rows and columns first. What it had no
answer for is the other question a reader has about a numeric column, which is *what shape is it*.

This is that answer, and it is thin — nine lines of column selection over [`Chart`](visualization.md#charts-kt-chart).
The interesting decision is which columns, and the rule is the one that makes `frame.chart()` with
no arguments do the obvious thing:

 - a **numeric** x column and the rest numeric: lines against it, one series per column;
 - a **categorical** first column (strings, or anything not numeric) and one numeric column: bars,
   with the category names on the axis — which is what a `groupBy(...).count()` looks like, and the
   commonest frame anyone actually plots;
 - no x column named and none obvious: the row index.

Non-numeric cells inside a numeric column become gaps rather than zeroes. A missing measurement is
not a measurement of zero, and drawing it as one is the single most common way a plot lies.

## DataFrameVisualizer.kt { #dataframevisualizer-kt }

Makes Kotlin DataFrame values render as Field values (`.h`, `.h2`, `display` and box return
values) without DataFrame having to know Field exists.

`DataFrame` is a third-party interface, so it cannot implement [`ToHTML`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt-tohtml) the way [`Table`](visualization.md#tables-kt-table) and [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img)
do. Both registries exist for exactly this: [`ValuePrinterRegistry`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt-valueprinterregistry) for the compact `.h` form, and
[`H2ValueRegistry`](visualization.md#lazyvaluevisualizer-kt-h2valueregistry) for `.h2`. Everything here is a thin adapter onto primitives that already exist,
so a frame gets the same styling, the same expander and the same paging as every other value.

### The compact `.h` form

`table` already renders a column-oriented table in Field's output style, so a frame's compact
form is that table over the first `HEAD_ROWS` rows, plus a line giving the shape. Only the head is
touched: each column is indexed for its first `HEAD_ROWS` cells rather than the frame being
materialised, so printing a million-row frame costs about what printing ten rows costs.

### The `.h2` scroller

[`H2ValueSnapshot`](visualization.md#lazyvaluevisualizer-kt-h2valuesnapshot) adapts one value into another for the lazy renderer rather than producing HTML.
So `.h2` on a frame adapts it into a private list-of-rows view that reads a row only when asked,
and the h2 explorer (`h2explorer.kt`, reached as an iframe onto `/h2-explorer?root=<token>` and fed
over the `/ws` `__h2_explorer__` channel) streams windows of it by index. The server holds the
frame rather than a rendering of it behind an `.h2` token, and each scroll materialises only the
window being looked at, which is what makes a large frame a scroller instead of a large HTML dump.
`ValueVisualizer`'s `/lazy-value-fragment` renderer is a separate path, for expanding a value in
place rather than scrolling one.

Going through the registries rather than a bespoke widget also means a frame nested inside another
value, a list of frames or a data class with a frame field, expands with the same machinery.

### Where the adapters get registered

`install` is idempotent and runs during server start-up. A bare `jvm-main` harness does not run
that, so tests call it explicitly; `DataFrameVisualizerSmokeTest` is the worked example.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/visualization/DataFrameVisualizer.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/visualization/DataFrameVisualizer/)

## H2DomainAdapters.kt { #h2domainadapters-kt }

`.h2` adapters for the Field types where the *reflective* default in `H2Reflect.kt` reads badly.

`H2Reflect` lifted `.h2` from "types someone registered" to "everything", and for a data class or
a plain domain object a property tree is exactly right. Four families it is wrong for, each for
its own reason:

 - **`Box`** — reflection would touch `Box.ki`, a `lazyVar` that *builds a K2 REPL engine on
   read*. Exploring a box would compile one. This is the concrete case behind the side-effect
   limit `H2Reflect`'s KDoc admits it cannot detect, and the reason `Box` is served here.
 - **`Functions.Fn`** — its only non-derived field is a private `(Double) -> Double`. A function's
   content is its *values*, so the adapter samples it.
 - **`FLine`** — a polyline's content is its node list, and `nodes` is one property among four.
 - **`Throwable`** — a `java.*` type, refused by the platform-package narrowing, and the value a
   box produces most often when something is wrong.

Each adapter returns a shape the existing explorer machinery already renders well —
a `LinkedHashMap` gets map paging, and a `List<Map<String, Any?>>` hits the explorer's RECORD
mode and becomes a real table with one column per key. That is deliberate: an adapter that
invented its own rendering would have to be maintained in three places.

## H2Reflect.kt { #h2reflect-kt }

The reflective half of `.h2`: what a domain object's *children* are, computed once and shared by
every surface that shows them.

`.h2` renders a value three separate times — the `Browsable` tree behind `/tree` and `/browse`,
the row/column stream behind the embedded `/h2-explorer` iframe, and the summary line in the
widget itself. This file computes the children all three read, reflectively and for any type. A
per-type [`H2ValueSnapshot`](visualization.md#lazyvaluevisualizer-kt-h2valuesnapshot) adapter is the alternative, and stays the route for a type whose
getters this cannot walk safely; without either, a non-collection falls through
`LazyValueVisualizer.visualize`'s opening guard to `ValueVisualizer` and `.h2` renders as `.h`.

`properties` is the *single* enumerator, so `/tree` and the iframe cannot disagree about how many
fields a value has.

### Getters are opaque

A `KProperty1` getter is opaque: there is no way to tell a field read from a computed property
that opens a file, allocates a GPU buffer or builds a K2 REPL engine. `Box.ki` is a `lazyVar`
that compiles on read, which is why `Box` is served by a hand-written adapter in
`H2DomainAdapters.kt` rather than by this file. The two narrowings in `readsWellInline` (platform
packages, and types whose `.h` rendering *is* the value) mitigate the general case rather than
settling it. If a type's getters are expensive or effectful, give it an adapter.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/visualization/H2Reflect.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/visualization/H2Reflect/)

## ImagingVisualizer.kt { #imagingvisualizer-kt }

Inline visualizers for the CPU imaging and computer-vision family (`afield.stdlib/imaging*.kt`):
what a gradient, a pyramid, a flow field or a list of corners looks like when a box evaluates one.

The imaging layer is around 250 public symbols of raster and feature code, and [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img) is the only
one of its types that carries a picture of its own. Everything else falls through to a reflective
object tree unless something here claims it, and there a list of forty [`Corner`](imaging.md#imaging-features-kt-corner)s is a wall of
`{x=…, y=…, response=…}` and a [`GaussianPyramid`](imaging.md#imaging-filters-kt-gaussianpyramid) is `GaussianPyramid@3f1a2b`. Those are exactly
the values you want to look at.

### Where this hooks in

Three one-line hooks, small enough that this file can grow without touching `ValueVisualizer.kt`:

 - `Img.toHTML` delegates to `img`. [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img) implements [`ToHTML`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt-tohtml), which `ValueVisualizer` dispatches
   before its built-in table, so improving the `Img` picture has to happen there.
 - `ValueVisualizer.visualizeBuiltIn`'s fallback branch tries `format` first, which covers the
   non-data classes ([`Gradient`](imaging.md#imaging-filters-kt-gradient), [`GaussianPyramid`](imaging.md#imaging-filters-kt-gaussianpyramid), [`LaplacianPyramid`](imaging.md#imaging-filters-kt-laplacianpyramid), [`FlowField`](imaging.md#imaging-geometry-kt-flowfield),
   [`ComponentLabelling`](imaging.md#imaging-features-kt-componentlabelling)).
 - `ValueVisualizer.formatList` tries `formatList` first, which covers the homogeneous detector
   outputs (`List<Corner>`, `List<HoughLine>`, `List<HoughCircle>`, `List<FlowVector>`,
   `List<Img>`).

### Turning a float image into pixels

The family is float-channel and unbounded: a Sobel `dx`, a Laplacian and a
difference-of-Gaussians are legitimately signed, an unnormalised response legitimately exceeds 1,
and a division somewhere upstream legitimately produces a NaN. A visualizer that clamps all of
those to `0..1` shows a flat white or a flat black rectangle and tells you nothing, so the raster
renderer picks one of three modes:

 - **direct** — every finite sample already sits in `0..1`. Shown as-is; nothing is rescaled.
 - **signed ±m** — some finite sample is negative. The range is made symmetric about zero
   (`m = max(|min|, |max|)`) so that zero is a fixed, recognisable colour. A 1-channel image is
   additionally run through the `coolwarm` diverging ramp from [`Colormaps`](visualization.md#colormaps-kt-colormaps) (blue negative, pale
   zero, red positive), because grey cannot carry the sign of a gradient. Multi-channel signed
   data is offset and scaled per sample without a ramp.
 - **auto-ranged** — everything is non-negative but the maximum exceeds 1. Linearly rescaled, with
   the data's true range printed beside it, so a bright pixel is never mistaken for 1.0.

The caption names the mode whenever the mode rescaled something; the statistics table inside the
disclosure names it in every case, including the fourth one, where no sample is finite at all.

Non-finite samples (NaN, ±∞) are counted, excluded from every statistic, and painted **magenta**
so they are impossible to miss. Excluding them is what keeps one NaN out of the minimum and the
maximum, where it would take the whole display range with it and quantise to a uniformly black
thumbnail captioned `range NaN…NaN`.

A 4-channel image is drawn over a **checkerboard**, so transparent and black are distinguishable.

### The disclosure

Each raster visualizer carries a closed `<details>` with the per-channel strip, a per-channel
histogram computed over the full-resolution samples, and the numeric stats. It is a plain
`<details>` element rather than a `lazy-value-fragment` expander link, so it needs no running
server and works identically in a live box, in a docs capture and in a saved HTML file.

## LazyValueVisualizer.kt { #lazyvaluevisualizer-kt }

The lazy half of value display: rather than inline a large structure, show one summary line plus
links into the server-side browsers.

`LazyValueVisualizer.visualize` — reached in a box as `h2` — passes anything small or
unrecognised straight to `ValueVisualizer`. For maps, lists, arrays and `FloatBuffer` /
`IntBuffer` it instead retains the value under a token and emits a summary, `outliner` and
`columns` links, and an embedded `/h2-explorer` iframe. Those tokens live in an in-memory
retention table (10 minutes, 256 entries), so the links only resolve against the running server
and go stale after that.

The private `Browsable` wrappers behind those routes page rather than copy: children are grouped
into range-labelled directories of at most 96 entries, and a map with more than 20,000 entries is
iterated on demand instead of snapshotted. `registerH2Value` adds a per-type adapter returning an
[`H2ValueSnapshot`](visualization.md#lazyvaluevisualizer-kt-h2valuesnapshot) when a type should be summarised or unwrapped differently, and
`lazyInlineExpanderHtml` is the inline "… +N more" link `ValueVisualizer` emits for elided
content.

## ValueVisualizer.kt { #valuevisualizer-kt }

The default value display for Field output areas: a Kotlin value in, a compact HTML fragment out.

`ValueVisualizer.visualize` is the entry point; `Any.h` and `Box.viz` are how it is usually
reached — `.h` hands back the fragment, `viz` displays it into a channel of a live box. A type
can take over its own rendering either by implementing [`ToHTML`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt-tohtml) or by registering a printer with
`registerValuePrinter`; both are trusted to return well-formed HTML, while ordinary strings,
characters, keys and reflected values are escaped here.

Output is bounded — [`ValueVisualizer`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt-valuevisualizer)'s own KDoc below covers dispatch order, the
built-in formatters and the size limits. Whatever those limits elide (the tail of a long string
or list, extra fields of an object) becomes an expander link, resolved later by
`renderLazyFragment` from the server's `/lazy-value-fragment` route, so the rest of the value is
only ever rendered if someone asks for it.

## charts.kt { #charts-kt }

Plots — the structure, the scales, and the one renderer for them.

[`Chart`](visualization.md#charts-kt-chart) is to a plot what [`Table`](visualization.md#tables-kt-table) is to a grid: build it, and it arrives on screen in the repo's
style with no markup in the way. It implements [`ToHTML`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt-tohtml), so `display(channel, chart)`, `chart.h`
and a box whose last expression is a `Chart` all render through `Chart.toHTML`; `Box.showChart`
is the terse form.

### This file or `plotly.kt`

`plotly.kt` — `showSignals`, `linePlot`, `scatter`, `violin` — is the default, and better at being
a chart: real text rather than glyph geometry, a plot that reflows to its panel instead of being
fitted and centred, and log, subplot and box axes this file does not carry. Reach for a [`Chart`](visualization.md#charts-kt-chart)
for the three things Plotly cannot do: composing a plot with other FLine geometry in one drawing
under a shared transform, picking, and `Chart.expect`.

Axis labels here are real glyph geometry (`labelLines`), filled and with their counters intact,
because `showPlaneGrid` has nowhere to put text. `niceTicks` is Heckbert's nice-number tick
algorithm in public. `dev_docs/chart_primitive.md` holds the Plotly comparison capture and the
survey of what each medium in the repo was drawing for itself.

### Marks pick themselves up

`Box.lines` switches to the interactive SVG renderer the moment any line carries
`FLine.onClick` or `FLine.hoverColor` (`someSkiko.kt`). Point and bar marks set both, so hovering
a bar and clicking a datum need no configuration — see `Chart.pickable` for the escape hatch and
the cost.

### Chart.expect

Exactly as in [`Table`](visualization.md#tables-kt-table). A plot in a doc or a live box usually carries a claim — "no residual
exceeds 1e-6", "every voice stayed inside the guard band". State the claim and it is *drawn* as a
band, the data outside it recolours, the footnote says how many points broke it, and
`Chart.deviations` hands the same list to a test.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/visualization/charts.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/visualization/charts/)

**Used in:** [Charts as FLines](../chart.md), [Filling a solid: tetrahedral meshing with TetGen](../tetgen.md)

## heatmap.kt { #heatmap-kt }

A rectangular array of numbers as a colour-mapped picture in a box output, in one call.

The file is two layers. `heatmapImage` is pure: a rectangular matrix in, a [`RasterImage`](visualization.md#heatmap-kt-rasterimage) of ARGB
pixels out, with the colour scale, the optional log transform, the bilinear upsample and the
overlay trace all resolved there, so a test or a docs capture can render one without a Box.
`Box.showHeatmap` adds the two steps a box wants, encoding to PNG and displaying it into an
output channel, and returns the bytes so the caller can save or re-display them. `Box.showImage`
is that same second layer over a pixel buffer you already have.

Two conventions decide which way up the picture comes out. The matrix is read row-major, outer
index the row and inner index the column, so rows are the vertical axis; and `flipY` defaults to
true, drawing row 0 at the bottom, which is what a spectrogram's frequency bins want. A
spectrogram stored the other way round, frame-outer and bin-inner, is the `transpose = true`
case: frames become x and bins become y.

Colour is a [`Colormaps`](visualization.md#colormaps-kt-colormaps) name and a range. Under `normalize` the range is the data's own minimum
and maximum; `vmin` and `vmax` pin it instead, which is what makes two captures comparable;
`logScale` runs each value through `log10(max(v, 1e-12))` first, for magnitude spectra and
anything else spanning orders of magnitude.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/visualization/heatmap.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/visualization/heatmap/)

## plotly.kt { #plotly-kt }

Plotly helpers — the short way to get a chart out of a box, wrapping `space.kscience.plotly`.

`linePlot`, `scatter`, `scatterSized` and `violin` cover the common shapes (lists of numbers,
`Vec2`, `Vec3`) and hand back a `Plot` already run through `darkMode`, the repo dark theme with
data-first margins. `showSignals` goes one step further: pass `"label" to values` pairs and it
traces them against a shared x with the `signalPalette`, optionally min-max normalized and with
dashed reference marks, then displays the plot into a channel of a live `Box` — it is already on
screen when it returns, so do not display it again.

`toHtml` renders a `Plot` into an HTML fragment via [`PlotlyIntegration`](visualization.md#plotly-kt-plotlyintegration). That fragment calls
`Plotly.react` in the browser, so the page has to have the Plotly library loaded already;
without it the fragment logs to the console and draws nothing.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/visualization/plotly.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/visualization/plotly/)

**Used in:** [Values over time: interpolants & keyframes](../interpolants_examples.md), [Springs, dampers, and a character with mass](../movement_examples.md), [Projecting a distance matrix](../projection_examples.md)

## tables.kt { #tables-kt }

Tabular output — the structure, and the one renderer for it.

[`Table`](visualization.md#tables-kt-table) is the counterpart of `showSignals` for data that is rows and columns rather than a
signal: build it, hand it to `Box.showTable` (or just let a box's last expression be one), and it
arrives on screen in the repo's output style. It implements [`ToHTML`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt-tohtml), so `ValueVisualizer`
dispatches it ahead of everything else — `display(channel, table)`, `table.h`, and a returned
`Table` all render through `Table.toHTML` with no extra wiring.

Why this exists: a box that wants a table has, until now, hand-rolled
`<table style='border-collapse:collapse…'>` with its own font stack, paddings and greys. A dozen
files under `src/` do exactly that and no two agree, which is a lot of markup standing between a
reader and what the box is actually saying.

The part that is not just formatting is `Table.expect`. A table in a doc or a live box usually
carries a *claim* — "every builder advanced one frame per pump", "no residual exceeds 1e-6" — and
a reader is otherwise asked to verify it by scanning cells. State the claim and the cells that
break it colour themselves, the footnote says how many did, and `Table.deviations` hands the same
list back to a test. That is the difference between showing a grid and showing an assertion you
can watch fail.

Trust model, same as the rest of value display: text produced by default formatting is escaped;
a string returned from a `Table.format` lambda is trusted HTML and inserted as-is.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/visualization/tables.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/visualization/tables/)

**Used in:** [Frames and the animation loop](../animation_time_model.md), [DataFrames in a Box](../dataframe.md), [How completions are ranked](../completion_ranking.md)

The semantic colour roles, shared with `markdown()`'s `{role:text}` spans — same six names, same `field-md-*` classes, so the same `--field-*` design token backs both. A cell that means "good" and a markdown span that means "good" are therefore the same colour by construction, and neither spells a hex literal.

Constants: `ACCENT`, `MUTED`, `DIM`, `OK`, `WARN`, `BAD`.
